channel.title: Mulder, It's Me
channel.description: Essays on The X-Files as film and television craft.

item.title: The Moving Element
item.description: Glen Morgan and James Wong wrote a Scully episode after viewers said she needed humanizing, and David Nutter shot it as two faces in a prison room. Beyond the Sea defines Scully's skepticism as a discipline held against her own grief.

item.title: The Voice Is the Edit
item.description: Robert Modell has no makeup, no effect and no dark to hide in. His power is a man talking, filmed as ordinary coverage, which puts the viewer in the same chair as his victims. Pusher is the hour where The X-Files came closest to admitting what a cut does.

item.title: The Editor Always Wins
item.description: Musings of a Cigarette Smoking Man is a story about a writer whose publisher changed his ending. Its own executives then changed its title, and its planned last shot vanished from the cut. The conspiracy, the episode admits, is one man's account of a history that had to include him.

item.title: The Frame Had a Ceiling
item.description: The X-Files was composed for the 4:3 television set, and the 2015 remaster that now streams everywhere opened it to 16:9. The wider picture adds a little at the sides and takes the top, and the top was where the show kept its fear.

item.title: Three Minutes Ahead of the Badge
item.description: The X-Files teaser showed the audience the thing before the agents ever heard of it. That made every case an exercise in dramatic irony, and rigged the show's central argument in Mulder's favor from the first scene.

item.title: A Crowd in the Room
item.description: The X-Files made its dread from two people, a flashlight and a cut. Ryan Coogler makes his from an unbroken camera moving through a full room. If the Hulu pilot carries his habits, that is a bigger break with the original than any new name on a badge.

item.title: Every Lie Gets the Same Lighting
item.description: In Jose Chung's From Outer Space, Rob Bowman shoots a power-line worker's screenplay with the same conviction as a hypnotized teenager's memory, and by the end the two agents are evidence in somebody else's file.

item.title: Series Order: Hulu Signs for a Season
item.description: Eight months after ordering a pilot, Hulu has picked up Ryan Coogler's X-Files to series. What the announcement confirms, what the trades report, what the blogs claim, and what the shape of the deal says about the show.

item.title: After the Basement: The Heirs Who Learned to End
item.description: In January 2007 the producers of Lost asked ABC for an end date and cited The X-Files as the reason. Vince Gilligan built Breaking Bad to be finite. The writers who came out of the X-Files room went on to make shows that could stop, and that is the part of the show's legacy least often counted.

item.title: The Case Against Mulder: I Want to Believe
item.description: The second X-Files film opened fourth, a week behind The Dark Knight, and the calendar has carried the blame ever since. The film deserves a harder look: it is the X-Files story that puts Mulder's faith on trial and rules for the skeptic.

item.title: Two Solos: What the Leads Did With the Camera
item.description: Handed the director's chair, David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson each made the same decision. They removed the other one. What the four episodes say about a partnership seen from inside.

item.title: Music Without an Address
item.description: Mark Snow produced thirty to thirty-five minutes of music for every episode of The X-Files, alone, on a Synclavier, for nine seasons. The underscore gave the unseen monster somewhere to live, and the two orchestral feature scores show what changed once the sound acquired a source.

item.title: The Paranoid Style, Renewed Weekly
item.description: The X-Files took its parking garages and sodium light from the conspiracy thrillers of the 1970s. Those films ended in defeat inside two hours. A weekly series needed paranoia that could come back on Friday, and the model for that was a cancelled ABC show about a Chicago reporter.

item.title: Who Holds the Camera
item.description: Seven episodes broke the show's format. Two of them, Chris Carter's, are an author showing his hand. The other five give the camera to a narrator nobody should trust: a novelist's informants, two bickering partners, a woman stuck in a Monday, a reality crew, the machines in a sushi bar.

item.title: The Wrong Whale: Post-Modern Prometheus and the Bride
item.description: Chris Carter's black-and-white fifth-season hour carries the marks of Bride of Frankenstein, the sequel James Whale made in 1935: a storyteller's frame, a monster who talks, a doctor played for camp, and an ending that refuses the tragedy its plot has set up.

item.title: Screwball on a Steadicam
item.description: Chris Carter built Triangle on Hitchcock's Rope, and the comparison has stuck. The episode's best act is a ten-minute chase through FBI headquarters that plays as farce, timed by a Steadicam instead of an editor.

item.title: Fight the Future Is Best When It Forgets It Is a Movie
item.description: The 1998 film spent its money on a spaceship under the ice and a helicopter over a cornfield. Its best scenes cost almost nothing, and they are the ones that still look like The X-Files.

item.title: Kim Manners Was Hired for Speed
item.description: Kim Manners directed 52 hours of The X-Files, more than anyone else, and the producers kept handing him the hours that had to move: the first comedy, the finales, the two-hour close. Home, the episode he is remembered for, was the exception.

item.title: Los Angeles Made the Look a Choice
item.description: In the summer of 1998 The X-Files left the rain for hard sun. The four Los Angeles seasons went on to collect two ASC awards and two Emmy nominations, and a photography that had arrived with the weather became something the crew had to build shot by shot.

item.title: The Light in the Character's Hand
item.description: Vancouver shot The X-Files dark because dark was cheap. Into that dark the show sent a handheld beam carried by a character, and for nine seasons the beam decided what the audience was allowed to know.
